newsitem.title: UK: RESEARCH ALERT-Morgan cuts Brazil GDP forecasts.
newsitem.headline: RESEARCH ALERT-Morgan cuts Brazil GDP forecasts.

text.p: Morgan Stanley Dean Witter said it was trimming previous growth forecasts for Brazil in 1997 and 1998 because of expected policy decisions that are likely to sacrifice growth for stability.

Morgan said it has revised downward its growth forecast to 3.4 percent from 3.6 percent for 1997. It also said it has sharply cut its growth estimate to 3.0 percent from previous figures of 4.8 percent for 1998.

"This important reduction reflects our belief that policymakers are willing to sacrifice growth to preserve stability, and our accompanying conclusion that they're going to have to do exactly this in an inconvenient time, election-year 1998," Ernest Brown, economist at Morgan Stanley said in a report.
In addition, Morgan Stanley said it had scaled back its expectations for sharp declines in interest rates in Brazil in 1997-1998.

"We think interest rates aren't going down much from current levels, and are going to use as our working forecasts an annualized central bank bond benchmark of 20 percent, yielding roughly 13 percent in real terms...," Brown said in the report.
At the same time, Morgan said it has also sharply reduced its expectations for inflation and devaluation of the Brazilian currency.
Morgan said it expects a 6.9 percent rise in consumer prices in 1997 compared with previous estimates of a rise of 7.8 percent.

The firm said it does not expect inflation to rise in 1998. "Tight money, the slowing economy, and productivity growth will likley provide the pricing needed to keep inflation at 6.2 percent for the year rather than our prior 10 percent," Brown said in the report.

Meanwhile, Morgan said it does not expect Brazilian authorities to make major changes to its current exchange rate regime, which the report said, has been to devalue the real at roughly 0.7 percent a month in recent months.
The U.S. investment bank said it expects pressure on the real to grow in the next 18 months, and assumes a monthly devaluation of 0.75 percent through 1998.

Given this scenario, Morgan said it expects the real to end 1997 at 1.12 to the dollar, stronger than its previous expectations of 1.14 to the dollar. It also expects the currency to end much stronger in 1998 at 1.20 to the dollar compared with previous estimates of 1.28 to the dollar.
